title: Exercise vs. Antidepressants: What a Major Study Found
description: A landmark 2024 study compared exercise to SSRIs for depression. The surprising results and what they mean for treatment decisions.

content.text: Can exercise really be as effective as medication for depression? A major 2024 meta-analysis provides the clearest answer yet—and the results may change how we think about treatment.

A BMJ meta-analysis of 218 randomized trials (14,170 participants) found that walking/jogging, yoga, and strength training significantly reduced depression symptoms, with effect sizes comparable to SSRIs.

items: Effects were dose-dependent—more intense exercise = better results

content.text: This doesn't mean exercise 'replaces' medication. Both work through different mechanisms and can be used together. For moderate depression, exercise may be a viable first option.
The findings suggest exercise should be a core part of depression treatment, not just a nice-to-have. It's not about choosing one over the other—it's about having more options.

Here's the catch: depression makes it hard to exercise. The symptoms—fatigue, low motivation, anhedonia—directly interfere with the treatment. This is why medication or therapy often needs to come first, creating enough improvement to make exercise possible.

items: Mild depression: Consider exercise as first-line treatment
Moderate depression: Exercise + therapy or medication
Severe depression: Usually medication/therapy first, add exercise when possible
Any exercise is better than none—start small
Aim for 150 minutes/week of moderate activity

content.text: Exercise is a legitimate treatment for depression with effects comparable to medication. It should be part of the conversation with your doctor. But it's not about replacement—it's about having multiple tools and finding what works for you.
